summary:
SPHEREx Sky Time Viewer is an astronomical web application connected directly to the official NASA/IPAC IRSA archive to explore, process, and analyze spectrophotometric and multi-epoch data from the NASA SPHEREx mission. Its primary goal is to enable rapid scientific screening and preliminary visual diagnostics of sky regions by downloading real Level-2 cutouts.

The platform supports automated queries by object name via CDS Sesame or coordinates (RA/Dec) via TAP/ADQL, alongside four synthetic demonstration scenarios. Once data is retrieved, it processes real FITS files by reprojecting them onto a common north-up grid, applying sub-pixel registration via FFT cross-correlation, and combining them with inverse-variance weighting to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

Users can inspect 102 spectral channels across six LVF detectors (0.74 to 5.1 µm) and extract interactive spectra from any sky coordinate, complete with molecular markers (H₂O, PAH, CO₂, CO) and CSV export. To detect variability, it compares epochs by subtracting only shared spectral channels (matched_pair), preventing false positives and classifying moving objects (SPX-MOV), transients (SPX-TRN), and variable stars (SPX-VAR), supported by Gaia DR2 and AllWISE overlays and a Python backend.
details:
SPHEREx SKTVR is a public web tool that lets anyone explore NASA SPHEREx infrared images of the sky and see how they change over time. Users pick a region of the sky by its coordinates, and the tool retrieves SPHEREx images of that region from different dates through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), aligns them, and shows the differences using blink comparison and a before/after slider. Stars and galaxies stay fixed, while objects that move or change brightness stand out immediately.

Moving objects can be cross-checked against known small bodies using JPL SBIdent and Horizons. Anything not matched is presented as a candidate for human review, never as a discovery. A spectrum view shows an object’s brightness across SPHEREx’s 102 near-infrared bands, with a plain-language note on what kind of body it resembles. A parallax explainer shows how far an object at 50, 100 or 500 AU would appear to shift between two observations six months apart, which is the principle behind searching for a distant Planet X.

Benefits

SPHEREx SKTVR removes the technical barrier to working with SPHEREx data: users need no programming and no knowledge of FITS files. It saves time by automating image retrieval and alignment, teaches concepts such as parallax and spectra with real data, and keeps scientific honesty by clearly separating candidates from confirmed detections.

Intended impact

The tool makes SPHEREx data accessible to students, educators and citizen scientists, in the spirit of earlier blink-comparison projects that engaged volunteers in searching for moving objects. It also offers astronomers a first-pass filter that flags moving objects worth follow-up. Its modular design (image source, alignment, change detection, catalog check, human review) could be adapted in future work to Earth observation tasks such as monitoring deforestation, flooding or fires.

Tools and technologies

Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx images), JPL SBIdent and JPL Horizons. Languages and libraries: Python (Astropy, NumPy) for data access and image processing, and JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web interface. Formats: FITS and WCS (World Coordinate System). The tool is deployed as a public web application. AI assistants were used to help us understand the underlying science and to draft documentation.

Creativity

We revive the blink comparator, the technique Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto, as a modern public tool. We pair it with spectra and a parallax explainer so users see both what changed and why it can be detected.

What our team considered

Physical limits: a cold body hundreds of AU away emits its own heat mostly in the far infrared, outside SPHEREx’s 0.75–5 µm range, so it could only be seen through very faint reflected sunlight. For that reason we do not claim to find Planet X; it is our scientific motivation, not a promised result. We treat false positives (cosmic rays, bad pixels, noise) by requiring detection across multiple observations and by matching candidates against known-object catalogs. We also considered accessibility (plain language and a glossary), performance with large files (using image cutouts and caching), and a clear label of which parts use real versus simulated data. A known limitation is that SPHEREx observes a given point in different colors at different times, which complicates building spectra for moving objects.
